s: Ignorance and delusion, origin of desire and Karman, are avoided for final deliverance; without delusion, misery ceases.
Desire originates ignorance and delusion, yet arises from delusion; it ends when greed and desire for sensory pleasures are absent.
Greed arises from desire, ends without property, and violent desire drives theft, deceit, falsehood, and continuing misery.
is_a misery Birth and death are rooted in Karman and are called misery. The teaching presents freedom from this cycle as part of final deliverance.
Women are presented as a serious obstacle to a Sramana seeking liberation and chastity, provoking carnal desire; he is instructed to avoid their attractions and houses they inhabit.

Colour is perceived by and attracts the eye. Pleasant colour causes love and unpleasant colour hatred; passionate desire or hatred brings ruin, pain, violence, dissatisfaction, greed, and misery, while dispassionate indifference frees a person from sorrow. As an aspect of development, it has five kinds: black, blue, red, yellow, and white.
Smell, one of five aspects of development, unfolds into two kinds: sweet-smelling substances and substances of bad smell.
Gñânâvaranîya is a Karman that obstructs right knowledge through five forms: sacred-book, perception, supernatural, thought-reading, and highest unlimited knowledge.
Darsanâvaranîya is a Karman that obstructs right faith, unfolding through nine kinds including sleep, activity, greed, and faith in specified objects of knowledge.
Vêdanîya, one of eight Karman kinds, leads to experiencing pleasure or pain, two forms with many subdivisions.

Môhanîya is a Karman, one of eight kinds, that leads to delusion. It unfolds in two aspects: faith, with three forms, right, wrong, and partly right and partly wrong, and conduct, with the four cardinal passions and other feelings. Its duration ranges from a part of a muhûrta to seventy Krores of Krores of Sâgarôpamâs.

Âyuhkarman is one of the eight kinds of Karman. It determines length of life and is fourfold, referring to denizens of hell, brute creation, men, and gods. Its duration ranges from a part of a muhûrta to thirty-three Krores of Krores of Sâgarôpamâs.
Antarâya is Karman, one of eight kinds, preventing entry to eternal bliss by fivefold obstruction of gifts, profit, momentary and continuous enjoyment, and power.

Lêsyâ is a Karman-produced state of the soul. It has six types, black, blue, grey, red, yellow, and white, with specified degrees, innumerable varieties, and durations. The unit describes its qualities, results, conjunction with, and leading to new existence, including conditions governing birth.

Black Lêsyâ is one of the lowest Lêsyâs. Rain-cloud coloured, bitter, foul-smelling, and harsh to touch, it develops in a person ruled by the five Âsravas, lacking the three Guptis, injuring living beings, and acting cruelly and violently. It brings the soul into miserable courses of life.

Blue Lêsyâ is one of the lowest Lêsyâs. Blue like Asôka, the Kasha’s tail, or lapis lazuli, it tastes intensely pungent. It develops in people marked by envy, anger, ignorance, deceit, greed, hatred, carelessness, pleasure-seeking, and sinful undertakings, bringing the soul into miserable courses of life.

Grey Lêsyâ is one of the lowest Lêsyâs, coloured like the Atasî flower, Kôkila feathers, or pigeons’ collars, and infinitely sour. It develops in dishonest, base, deceitful, heretical, hurtful, sinful, thieving, jealous people and brings the soul into miserable courses of life.

Red Lêsyâ is a good Lêsyâ, vermilion like the rising sun or a parrot’s bill, with a pleasant taste. It develops in a humble, disciplined, law-loving person and brings the soul into happy courses of life.

Yellow Lêsyâ is a good Lêsyâ, coloured like orpiment, turmeric, or Sana and Asana flowers and tasting infinitely better than wine, liquors, honey, and Mairêyaka. It develops in calm, self-controlled people with little anger, pride, deceit, and greed, bringing the soul into happy courses of life.

White Lêsyâ is a good Lêsyâ, conch-shell-colored and infinitely sweeter than dates, grapes, milk, and sugars. It develops in a calm, self-controlled, meditative, sense-subduing man who meditates on Law and truth and practises Samitis and Guptis, bringing the soul into happy courses of life.

l: miserable courses of life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: are_reached_through black Lêsyâ [also through blue and grey Lêsyâs] Miserable courses of life are the courses into which the soul is brought through the black, blue, and grey Lêsyâs.

l: happy courses of life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: are_reached_through red Lêsyâ [also through yellow and white Lêsyâs] Happy courses of life are the courses into which the soul is brought through the red, yellow, and white Lêsyâs.
Pravragyâ is taken when a sage gives up life in a house. In taking it, the sage should know and renounce the attachments that take hold of men.
is_a great sin Buying makes a monk a buyer, and selling makes him a merchant. A monk should not engage in buying and selling because it is a great sin.
Things without life are constituents of world and solely comprise Non-world; divided into formless and form-possessing things, they are described through substance, place, time, and development.
contains Things without life [only] The Non-world (Alôka) is the space where only Things without life are found. Space fills both the Non-world (Alôka) and the world (Lôka).
Formless things, a division of Things without life, comprise ten kinds: Dharma, Adharma, space and time, including their divisions and indivisible parts.

Things possessing form are without life and have four kinds: compound things, their divisions, indivisible parts, and atoms. Their development flows without beginning or end, while each individual has a beginning and end. Duration ranges from one Samaya to an immeasurable period, with interruptions from one Samaya to endless time.
Taste, an aspect of development, unfolds into five kinds: bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, and sweet.
Touch, one of five aspects of development, unfolds through eight kinds: hard, soft, heavy, light, cold, hot, smooth, and rough.
Figure, one of five aspects of development, unfolds into five kinds: globular, circular, triangular, square, and long.

Perfected souls are living beings including women, men, hermaphrodites, orthodox, heterodox, and householders. On reaching perfection they go to Îshatprâgbhâra at the world's top, barred from Alôka, formless, living, knowing, faithful, and incomparably happy.
Îshatprâgbhâra is a pure, white-gold place twelve Yôganas above Sarvârtha where perfected souls go, shaped like an open umbrella, vast in length and breadth, and thickest at its middle.
Sarvârtha is the Vimâna above which Îshatprâgbhâra is located. In the great Vimâna Sarvârtha(siddha), the duration of life is always thirty-three Sâgarôpamâs.

is_a three kinds [Earth Lives, Water Lives, and plants] Immovable living beings are of three kinds: Earth Lives, Water Lives, and plants. Each kind is divided into subtile and gross forms, which may be fully developed or undeveloped.
Water Lives are immovable beings lasting seven thousand years, unfolding as subtile or gross, developed or undeveloped forms including water, dew, fog, and ice.
Fire Lives are movable beings, subtile or gross and developed or undeveloped; gross developed forms include flame, lightning, meteors, coal, and chaff.
Wind Lives are movable beings, subtle or gross and developed or undeveloped; gross developed forms include winds, squalls, whirlwinds, and Samvartaka wind.

l: beings with five organs of sense, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Beings with five organs of sense are movable organic beings: denizens of hell, animals, men, and gods, distinguished by subdivisions, habitats, and life durations.

lead_to bad births [Kandarpa-, Abhiyôgika-, Kilvisha-, Môha-, and Asuratva-Bhâvanâs] The Kandarpa-, Abhiyôgika-, Kilvisha-, Môha-, and Asuratva-Bhâvanâs lead to evil ways and are obnoxious at the time of death. Their practices include ribaldry, spells, reviling sacred beings, anger, prognostics, and prohibited acts.

is_reached_by orthodox opinions [at the time of death, by souls that do not commit sins and have white Lêsyâ] Souls with heretical opinions, sins, and killing do not reach Bôdhi at death. Souls with orthodox opinions, no sins, and white Lêsyâ reach Bôdhi at death.
delivered Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana [the enlightened and liberated author] The enlightened and liberated Gñâtri(putra) delivered the Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana.

l: Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: was_delivered_by Gñâtri(putra) [the enlightened and liberated] The Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana were delivered by the enlightened and liberated Gñâtri(putra). The pious approve of them.

The Kalpa Sûtra presents the lives, eras, lineages, and monastic rules associated with the Ginas and Tîrthakaras, culminating in regulations for religious communities. It begins with Mahâvîra, the last Tîrthakara: his embryo first enters Devânandâ’s womb in Kundagrâma, then, by Sakra’s order, Harinegamesi transfers it to the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ. Both women’s dreams signal an extraordinary son; Trisalâ’s fourteen auspicious dreams are identified as those seen by every mother of a Tîrthakara. Siddhârtha and dream interpreters understand them to foretell either a universal emperor or a Gina. Mahâvîra remains still in Trisalâ’s womb to protect her from anxiety, later moves, and resolves not to become houseless while his parents live. After nine months and seven and a half days he is born, named Vardhamâna by his parents and Mahâvîra by the gods. He renounces property and household life, practises austerity for more than twelve years, attains Kevala in his thirteenth year, and dies at Pâpâ, becoming Siddha, Buddha, and Mukta; Indrabhûti attains Kevala that same night. The work notes differing chronological reckonings since his death and closes his life. It next recounts Pârsva’s life, from birth in Benares through renunciation with three hundred men, Kevala after eighty-four days, and liberation on mount Sammeta; then Arishtanemi’s life, liberation on mount Girnâr, followers, and chronology. The epochs of intermediate Tîrthakaras calculate immense intervals since Nami, Munisuvrata, Malli, Sîtala, and others. Rishabha’s life follows: he teaches arts and occupations, installs his hundred sons as kings, renounces, attains Kevala, establishes a fourfold community, and is liberated on mount Ashtâpada. A list of Sthaviras traces Mahâvîra’s nine Ganas, eleven Ganadharas, and later spiritual succession from Ârya-Sudharman through named teachers. Finally, the Rules for Yatis prescribe Paggusan observance: residence, travel, alms, diet, clothing, cleanliness, speech, disputes, and care for small living beings. Mahâvîra proclaims the Paryushanâkalpa, ending both the rules and the Kalpa Sûtra.

Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra is the last Tîrthakara, of the Gñâtri Kshatriya race and Kâsyapa gotra, son of Siddhârtha and associated with the names Vardhamâna and Sramana. His life unfolds from descent from the great Vimâna Pushpottara through conception: he first takes embryonic form in Devânandâ’s womb and is transferred to Trisalâ’s womb. Brought into the Gñâtri family, he is called Vardhamâna because its wealth and prosperity increase. While still in the womb, he remains motionless to avoid troubling his mother, moves when he learns her sorrow, and resolves not to become houseless while his parents live. He is born a healthy boy in Kundapura. After thirty years as a householder, he leaves property, kingdom, and possessions, practices asceticism and meditation, and after more than twelve years below perfection attains Kevala: supreme, complete knowledge and intuition. Thereafter he is a Kevalin, Gina, and Arhat, establishes a large community with nine Ganas and eleven Ganadharas, and has Indrabhûti as oldest disciple. He commences Paggusan and proclaims Paryushanâkalpa at Râgagriha’s Kaitya Gunasilaka. After under thirty years as a Kevalin, within a lifespan of seventy-two years, he dies in Pâpâ as a Siddha, liberated and freed from pains; his final liberation is in Svâti.

Brâhmanî Devânandâ, of the Gâlandharâyana gotra and wife of Rishabhadatta, first carries Mahâvîra’s embryo in her womb. In a state between sleeping and waking, she experiences the fourteen great dreams. On the night the embryo is removed, she sees the dreams taken from her by the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ and awakens.

Sakra is chief and king of the gods, commanding them from his celestial abode and throne, riding Airavata and wielding the thunderbolt. After perceiving Mahâvîra’s conception through Avadhi, he orders Harinegamesi to transfer the embryo from Devânandâ to Trisalâ because Tîrthakaras are born in high families.
Divine commander of the foot troops who, at Sakra's command, transfers Mahâvîra's embryo to Trisalâ and places Trisalâ's embryo in Devânandâ.

Kshatriyânî Trisalâ is a Kshatriyânî of the Vâsishtha gotra and wife of Siddhârtha. Her womb receives the embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra after its transfer. That night, during pregnancy, she sees fourteen illustrious, auspicious great dreams and awakens joyfully. She asks Siddhârtha what they portend, accepts his and the dream interpreters’ interpretation, carefully carries her unborn child, and gives birth to Mahâvîra as a perfectly healthy boy.

Siddhârtha is a Kshatriya king of the Kâsyapa gotra, husband of Trisalâ and father of Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra. After Trisalâ’s fourteen dreams, he consults dream interpreters, honours them, and tells her their prediction of an exceptional son.
The Arhats are revered in opening obeisances and Sakra’s praise; across past, present, and future, they are born or moved at conception into high, noble, royal, or pure families.
are conquerors who have conquered fear The Ginas are praised as conquerors who have conquered fear, reached the path of perfection, and are liberated and liberators.
The Tîrthakaras are perfectly enlightened guides and benefactors, unfolding through twenty-three earlier figures to Mahâvîra, their last.

include Suras [as a designation] The gods include Sakra and the divine beings under his command. They enjoy permitted divine pleasures, and Harinegamesi uses divine motion and transformation to carry out Sakra's order.
contains Bharatavarsha Gambûdvîpa is the continent where Mahâvîra's conception and embryo transfer take place. It contains Bharatavarsha and the town of Kundagrâma.
Bharatavarsha is the region within Gambûdvîpa where Kundagrâma is located and where Mahâvîra takes the form of an embryo.
Kundagrâma, a town in Bharatavarsha, has brahmanical and Kshatriya parts containing Devânandâ’s and Siddhârtha and Trisalâ’s houses, where Mahâvîra is conceived.

l: the brahmanical part of Kundagrâma, Kalpa Sutra
s: The brahmanical part of Kundagrâma is where Devânandâ and Rishabhadatta dwell. Mahâvîra's embryo is first placed there and is later removed from it.

l: the Kshatriya part of Kundagrâma, Kalpa Sutra
s: contains the womb of Devânandâ [at Siddhârtha's house after the transfer] The Kshatriya part of Kundagrâma is where Siddhârtha and Trisalâ dwell. Harinegamesi places Mahâvîra's embryo in Trisalâ's womb there.
Uttaraphalgunî is an asterism joined with the moon throughout Mahâvîra’s descent, conception, transfer, birth, renunciation, and Kevala.

l: Mahâvîra's descent from heaven, Kalpa Sutra
s: Mahâvîra's descent from heaven occurred when the moon was in conjunction with Uttaraphalgunî. He descended from the Vimâna Pushpottara after his divine existence had reached its termination. Rishabha descended from the great Vimâna called Sarvârthasiddha after living there for thirty-three Sâgaropamas. His descent occurred in the dark fortnight of Ashâdha on its fourth day, when the moon was in conjunction with Uttarâshâdhâ.
Mahâvîra's conception occurs at midnight under Uttaraphalgunî, beginning as an embryo in Devânandâ's womb before the transfer.

l: the transfer of Mahâvîra's embryo, Kalpa Sutra
s: On Sakra’s command, Harinegamesi transfers Mahâvîra’s embryo at midnight under Uttaraphalgunî from Devânandâ’s womb to Trisalâ’s, exchanging it with Trisalâ’s embryo.

Mahâvîra's birth is an event at king Siddhârtha's palace in Kundapura. After nine months and seven and a half days, during the first month of summer, on the fourteenth day of Kaitra's dark fortnight, Trisalâ gives birth at midnight to a healthy boy while the moon is joined with Uttaraphalgunî. Divine lustre, noise from gods and goddesses, and riches mark the birth. His parents name him Vardhamâna, and a ten-day festival celebrates it.

Mahâvîra's renunciation is his departure from household life into houselessness. When he perceived the time had come, he abandoned wealth, kingdom, army, household, and possessions; in Shandavana of the Gñâtris, under the Asoka tree, he removed ornaments, plucked out his hair, left the house, and entered houselessness under Uttaraphalgunî.

Kevala is the highest knowledge and intuition: infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and perfect or full. Mahâvîra obtained it under Uttaraphalgunî during his thirteenth year; Indrabhûti attained it on the night of Mahâvîra's death. Pârsva attained it under a Dhâtaki tree on the eighty-fourth day after entering houselessness. Arishtanemi attained it fifty-five days after renunciation and lived nearly seven centuries as a Kevalin. Rishabha reached it after fasting three and a half days and deep meditation.
Mahâvîra's final liberation occurred under Svâti after he died in Pâpâ; freed from all pains, he became a Siddha, Buddha, and Mukta.

l: the fourteen great dreams, Kalpa Sutra
s: The fourteen great dreams are fourteen auspicious dreams, numbered among the thirty great dreams in dream-books and associated with mothers of universal monarchs or Arhats. They are seen by Kshatriyânî Trisalâ and include, in order, an elephant, bull, lion, Srî, flower garland, moon, sun, flag, vase, Lotus Lake, milk-ocean, celestial abode, jewel heap, and fire. They are described as illustrious, beautiful, lucky, blest, and fortunate. A parallel account says Devânandâ saw the same dreams between sleeping and waking. The dreams of Kshatriyânî Trisalâ portend the birth of a son who will become a universal emperor or a Gina.

l: embryo of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra (in Trisalâ's womb), Kalpa Sutra
s: Mahâvîra’s embryo is first placed in Devânandâ’s womb, then removed during a transfer and placed in Trisalâ’s womb. Trisalâ carries it during pregnancy; the embryo remains motionless compassionately to spare her distress.

l: the womb of Devânandâ, Kalpa Sutra
s: The womb of Devânandâ first received Mahâvîra's embryo. Harinegamesi later removed Mahâvîra's embryo from it and placed the embryo of Trisalâ there.

see fourteen dreams (of Kshatriyânî Trisalâ) [when a famous Arhat enters the womb] The text states that every mother of a Tîrthakara sees these fourteen dreams on the night in which the famous Arhat enters her womb.

Dream interpreters, versed in prognostics and many sciences, are summoned to Siddhârtha’s palace to interpret Trisalâ’s fourteen dreams. Consulting dream-books, they foretell a universal emperor or a Gina; Siddhârtha honours them with gifts and dismisses them.

is_a town [containing the Kshatriya quarter] Kundapura was the town where the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was born. King Siddhârtha ordered it to be decorated, cleaned, supplied with festivities, and filled with performers and celebrations for the birth.
Dream-books enumerate forty-two common and thirty great dreams, fourteen of which mothers of universal monarchs or Arhats see when an embryo enters the womb.
Vardhamâna, a Gñâtri Kshatriya and prince of Videha, was named by his parents after their wealth and possessions increased following his birth.

Indrabhûti, of the Gautama gotra, was the oldest monk and disciple of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, a Ganadharas who instructed five hundred Sramanas. On the night of his master’s death he cut his tie of friendship for his master and attained Kevala; he died after Mahâvira’s Nirvâna.

Sramanas are ascetics who follow the Law defended by Mahâvîra and communities associated with Rishabha. Their communities are led by named heads and range from fourteen thousand under Indrabhûti to sixteen thousand under Âryadatta for Pârsva and eighty-four thousand under Rishabhasena for Rishabha. They include sages and disciples with specified attainments. During Kshudrâtma’s stay in Mahâvîra’s natal asterism, respect and honour for Sramanas, Nirgrantha monks, and nuns decline.

l: Mahâvîra's attainment of Kevala, Kalpa Sutra
s: occurs_in field of the householder Sâmâga [under a Sal tree outside Grimbhikagrâma on the river Rigupâlika] After meditating for twelve years, the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra attained the highest knowledge and intuition called Kevala during his thirteenth year. He became a Gina, Arhat, and Kevalin, omniscient and comprehending all objects and conditions of living beings.

The Nirvâna of Mahâvira is the final liberation of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra. During the last night of the rainy season, he died in king Hastipâla's office of the writers in Pâpâ, was freed from pains, cut asunder the ties of birth, old age, and death, and became finally liberated. It became a point for counting elapsed time; Indrabhûti, Ârya Sudharman, and the Ganadharas died afterward.

fourfold Karman includes Vedanîya and is suppressed by Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra through exertion and meditation; before final liberation, Karman producing Vedanîya, Âyus, name, and family was exhausted at his death.

l: Law of the Sramanas, Kalpa Sutra
s: benefits all living beings [throughout the whole universe] The Laukântika gods urged the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra to establish the religion of the law benefiting all living beings. During his renunciation, he was also urged to defend the conquered Law of the Sramanas.

is_practiced_by Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra [with circumspection and without possessions] The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra entered the state of houselessness after leaving his home and tearing out his hair. He later walked naked, accepted alms in the hollow of his hand, guarded his thoughts, words, and acts, and endured pleasant and unpleasant occurrences with equanimity.
elapsed_since death of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira Nine centuries are said to have elapsed since the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died.

is_replaced_by ninety-third year [in another redaction] The eightieth year is identified as the current year of the tenth century since the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira died. Another redaction gives the ninety-third year instead.
has_ended end The Fifth Lecture ends in this unit.
has_ended end The Life of Mahâvîra ends in this unit.

Pârsva is an Arhat and the people’s favourite. After living in Prânata Kalpa for twenty Sâgaropamas, he descends and is conceived, is born in Benares as Vâmâ’s son, and lives thirty years as a householder. He leaves home by tearing out his hair, renounces in Visâlâ, travels to Asramapada followed by gods, men, and Asuras, and approaches Asoka. After fasting without water, he attains Kevala under a Dhâtaki tree. He has eight ganas and ganadharas and large communities of Sramanas, nuns, and lay votaries. He lives something less than seventy years as a Kevalin, dies on mount Sammeta after a month’s fast, and obtains final liberation in Visâkhâ.

Nuns during the Paggusan follow Yati rules governing residence, travel, alms, food, cleanliness, inspection, lodging, speech, disputes, and movement. They extend residence and collect alms within a Yogana and Krosa, need three lodging-places and pots, limit drinks, and cannot accept unrequested food or drink.
Benares was the town in Bharatavarsha where Pârsva descended, was conceived, and was born. Pârsva later traveled through Benares to the park called Asramapada when he renounced the household life.

Visâkhâ was the asterism in conjunction with the moon during Pârsva's descent and conception, birth, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, and final liberation. These were described as the five most important moments of his life.
is_a life event Pârsva obtained final liberation when the moon was in conjunction with Visâkhâ. He later died on the summit of mount Sammeta, freed from all pains.
Pârsva descends from the Prânata Kalpa after twenty Sâgaropamas and becomes an embryo in Vâmâ’s womb in Benares.
Birth of Pârsva: after nine months and seven and a half days, Vâmâ gives birth in Benares to a perfectly healthy boy under Visâkhâ.
Pârsva’s life event of renunciation occurs in Visâkhâ: after fasting three and a half days, he tears out his hair with three hundred men and enters houselessness.

is_a life event Pârsva attained Kevala on the eighty-fourth day after entering houselessness. He fasted two and a half days without drinking water and reached the highest knowledge and intuition under a Dhâtaki tree.

is_a life event Pârsva died on the summit of mount Sammeta after fasting a month without drinking water. His death occurred during the light fortnight of Srâvana, with the moon in conjunction with Visâkhâ, and he was freed from all pains.

is_a life account The Life of Pârsva describes his descent, conception, birth, household life, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, community, epochs, death, and final liberation. It states that twelve centuries had elapsed since his death and that the thirteenth century was in its thirtieth year.

lasts_for eighty-three days [a state inferior to perfection] Pârsva entered houselessness after tearing out his hair and remained there for eighty-three days before attaining Kevala. During this period he neglected his body, was circumspect, and meditated upon himself.
is_a life account The Life of Arishtanemi recounts his descent from heaven, birth, renunciation, attainment of Kevala, teachings, death, and final liberation.

Arhat Arishtanemi descended from Aparâgita into Gambûdvîpa and Bharatavarsha, took embryonic form in Queen Sivâ, and was born in Sauripura as King Samudravigaya’s son. After a life lasting a thousand years, he renounced at Revatîka with a thousand persons, followed by gods, men, and Asuras. He obtained Kevala, led eighteen Ganas and eighteen Ganadharas with large communities, then died on mount Girnâr after a month’s fast and attained final liberation.
Arishtanemi's birth in Sauripura begins with embryo formation in queen Sivâ's womb and ends nine months later with the healthy boy's birth.

is_a renunciation [entry into the state of houselessness] Arishtanemi renounced the world in the park Revatîka after fasting for two and a half days without drinking water. Under the asterism Kitrâ, he tore out his hair with a thousand persons and entered the state of houselessness.

On mount Girnâr, Arishtanemi attained infinite knowledge and intuition called Kevala under a Vetasa tree. He later died on its summit after fasting for a month without drinking water, in the company of five hundred and thirty-six monks.
Sramanas are an excellent community of eighteen thousand led by Varadatta, within Arishtanemi’s wider community of sages and disciples.

is_a death [followed by freedom from all pains] Arishtanemi died on the summit of mount Girnâr in the middle of the night when the moon was in conjunction with Kitrâ. He fasted for a month without drinking water and died in a squatting position surrounded by five hundred and thirty-six monks.

follows Arishtanemi's death [freedom from all pains] After his fourfold Karman was exhausted, Arishtanemi was freed from all pains and obtained final liberation. Since his death, eighty-four thousand years and part of the eighty-fifth millennium had elapsed.

l: Epochs of the Intermediate Tîrthakaras, Kalpa Sutra
s: is_a chronological account The epochs record elapsed years since the deaths of Arhat Nami, Munisuvrata, and Malli, and give chronological intervals between several Tîrthakaras. They include the relative dates of Sîtala, Vîra, and earlier Tîrthakaras.
dies deceased Arhat Nami’s death is used as a chronological starting point. Since his death, 584,979 years have elapsed, and this is the eightieth year.
dies deceased The chronology states that the current year is 1,184,980 since Munisuvrata’s death.

dies deceased The chronology states that the current year is 6,584,980 since Malli’s death. Ara died 10,000,000 years before Malli, while Kunthua, Sânti, Dharma, Ananta, Vimala, Vâsupûgya, and Sreyâmsa died progressively earlier by the intervals specified.
Sîtala is a person whose death occurred a krore of Sâgaropamas less 42,003 years and eight and a half months before Vîra’s death, after named predecessors.

has_death_after Sîtala [by a krore of Sâgaropamas less 42,003 years and eight and a half months] Vîra’s death is used as the reference point for Sîtala’s death. Sîtala died a krore of Sâgaropamas less 42,003 years and eight and a half months before Vîra.

Rishabha, a Kosalian Arhat of the Kâsyapa gotra, is called First King, First Mendicant, First Gina, and First Tîrthakara. Descending from Sarvârthasiddha, he was born to Nâbhi and Marudevî in Bharatavarsha and Ikshvâkubhûmi. He spent two millions of former years as a prince and six millions three hundred thousand as king, teaching sciences, arts, accomplishments, and occupations. He had a hundred sons, anointed them as kings, then renounced with four thousand royal persons and Kshatriyas. After one thousand years short of perfection, he attained Kevala and established a large fourfold community with Sramanas, nuns, lay votaries, and female lay votaries, alongside sages, Kevalins, Ganas, and Ganadharas. He died with ten thousand monks at mount Ashtâpada in Samparyaṅka position, attained final liberation, and was freed from all pains.

After descending from heaven, Rishabha took the form of an embryo in the womb of Marudevî, wife of the patriarch Nâbhi. Marudevî saw dreams, including a bull coming forward with his face, and Nâbhi himself interpreted them.

Marudevî gave birth to a perfectly healthy boy, Rishabha, in the dark fortnight of Kaitra on its eighth day. The circumstances connected with his birth were otherwise the same as those of Mahâvîra, except that the contents of §§ 100 and 101 did not apply.

Rishabha lived six millions three hundred thousand former years as a king. During his reign he taught the seventy-two sciences, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men, and he anointed his hundred sons as kings, giving each a kingdom.

Rishabha left the town Vinîtâ for Siddhârtha Vana, tore out his hair with four thousand royal persons and Kshatriyas, and entered the state of houselessness. He began this renunciation in the first month of summer, in the dark fortnight of Kaitra on its eighth day.

After neglecting his body and meditating upon himself for one thousand years, Rishabha fasted three and a half days and attained Kevala outside Purimatâla, in the park called Sakatamukha, under the tree Nyagrodha.

Rishabha died on the summit of mount Ashtâpada in the company of ten thousand monks, after fasting six and a half days without drinking water. His death occurred in the dark fortnight of Mâgha on its thirteenth day, when the moon was in conjunction with Abhigit.
Rishabha obtained final liberation when the moon was in conjunction with Abhigit. After his fourfold Karman was exhausted, he was freed from all pains.

Life of Rishabha traces his descent, conception, birth, long life as prince, king, and householder, then renunciation, attainment of Kevala, death, and final liberation. His total life spans eight millions four hundred thousand years, including time inferior to perfection and as a Kevalin.
Ârya-Sudharman, an Agnivesyâyana Sthavira and Ganadhara, instructed five hundred Sramanas, died after Mahâvira’s Nirvâna, and is spiritual ancestor of present Nirgrantha Sramanas.

The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra had nine Ganas. Later Ganas, including those founded by Godâsa, Uttara and Balissaha, Rohana, Bhadrayasas, Kâmarddhi, Srîgupta, Rishigupta Kâkandaka, and Susthita and Supratibuddha, are described with their Sâkhâs and Kulas.

Ganadharas were eleven disciples of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, knowing twelve Aṅgas, fourteen Pûrvas, and the Siddhânta of the Ganins. After commencing Paggusan, they died following a month’s fast without water and left no descendants.
The Nirgrantha Sramanas are present spiritual descendants of Ârya-Sudharman; following earlier teachers and the Sthaviras, they commence Paggusan after a month and twenty rainy-season nights.

The Sthaviras are a succession of teachers from Ârya-Sudharman through many named figures, whose disciples founded Ganas and Sâkhâs and preserved sacred lore. Praised for virtue and self-restraint, they follow rainy-season conduct and Paggusan restrictions on requests, hair, lodging, and behavior.
Ârya Bhadrabâhu of the Prâkîna gotra had four Kâsyapa-gotra disciples, beginning with Godâsa, who founded the divided Godâsa Gana.

Ârya Mahâgiri of the Ailâpatya gotra had eight disciples, whose founders established the Uttarabalissaha Gana and Trairâsika Sâkhâ.

Paggusan is a rainy-season observance, normally begun after a month and twenty nights, though earlier commencement is allowed. It unfolds through detailed rules governing monks’ and nuns’ residence, travel, alms, food, conduct, lodging, and reconciliation.

The rainy season determines the customary commencement of the Paggusan after a month and twenty nights have elapsed. During it, living beings, grass, seeds, mildew, and sprouts frequently come forth, requiring monks and nuns to inspect places carefully.

Monks during the Paggusan follow rules for residence, travel, alms, diet, permissions, cleanliness, inspection, lodging, speech, disputes, and movement. They range within a Yogana and a Krosa, collect alms at a fixed time with a teacher’s permission, eat one meal daily, and limit drinks when healthy. Longer fasts permit hot pure water. They restrict house visits, use an alms-bowl, seek permission for cures and exalted penance, and maintain three lodging-places, inspected easing spots, and three pots to support control.

Householders prepare and clean their houses before the customary commencement of the Paggusan. Converted and devoted householders honour, praise, and permit visits by monks, but are not to be prompted about things that are not seen because they might buy or steal them.
Âkârya is a superior who, during the Paggusan, directs food giving and acceptance for sick brothers and grants permission for monks’ activities.

Whom he knows as a dweller on high, him he should know as a dweller far (from sin) and whom he knows as a dweller far (from sin), him he should know as a dweller on high. Man! restraining thyself (from the outward world) 'thou wilt get free from pain.' Man, understand well the truth! exerting himself in the rule of truth a wise man overcomes Mâra. This is the doctrine of the Seer who does not injure living beings and has put an end (to acts and to samsâra). Preventing propensity to sin destroys former actions. He who knows one thing, knows all things; and he who knows all things, knows one thing. He who is careless in all respects, is in danger; he who is not careless in all respects, is free from danger. (1) He who conquers one (passion), conquers many; and he who conquers many, conquers one. 'Knowing the misery of the world' rejecting the connection with the world, 'the heroes go on the great journey,' they rise gradually; 'they do not desire life.' (3) He who knows wrath, knows pride; he who knows pride, knows deceit; he who knows deceit, knows greed; he who knows greed, knows love; he who knows love, knows hate; he who knows hate, knows delusion; he who knows delusion, knows conception; he who knows conception, knows birth; he who knows birth, knows death; he who knows death, knows hell; he who knows hell, knows animal existence; he who knows animal existence, knows pain. Therefore, a wise man should avoid wrath, pride, deceit, greed, love, hate, delusion, conception, birth, death, hell, animal existence, and pain.
